description: We are a team passionate about space, science, and technology, building an interactive platform to explore and compare lunar landing sites. We welcome motivated teammates skilled in Python, web development, data analysis, GIS, or design. Beginners are welcome!
summary: AstroNova is a web application that finds the best site and the best time to operate at the Moon's south pole: when a lander has sunlight for solar power and the Earth in view for direct communication, at the same time. At the south pole the Sun never rises more than about 1.6° above the horizon and the Earth only about 7°, so a single ridge can cut power, communication or both. As the challenge notes, tools that compute Sun and Earth positions exist, but their complicated interfaces make critical information hard to evaluate efficiently. AstroNova answers this with a simple three-step interface. Users pick candidate sites, dates and a priority, and with one click get the best site and the longest shared window, with a plain-language "Why?". Every result is computed from NASA LOLA terrain and the JPL DE421 ephemeris, including each site's real mountain horizon. The tool runs free in any browser. This matters because faster, clearer site and timing decisions reduce risk for CLPS and Artemis missions, and make lunar planning accessible to researchers and students.
details:
What it does

AstroNova helps mission planners decide where and when to operate at the lunar south pole. It has three steps: (1) Mission Window Finder – choose sites, dates and a priority (power, communication or both) and get the best site and the longest window with sunlight and Earth visibility together, with a plain "Why?"; (2) Lunar Map – real NASA terrain in 2-D and 3-D with slope, sunlight and Earth-visibility layers; (3) Mission Console – for any moment and place, see the Sun and Earth in the sky, the mountain horizon, and the time until sunset or Earthrise.

How it works

Sun and Earth positions come from the NASA JPL DE421 ephemeris, rotated into the Moon's frame with the IAU 2009 model. For each site, 360 rays are traced across the NASA LOLA elevation map (including lunar curvature) to get the real mountain horizon. The Sun gives power when it is above that horizon; the Earth gives a link when it is above it. A mission window is when both are true. Sites are scored by the longest shared window and the share of time with power and link.

Validation

The engine found the published sunniest peaks (Bussey et al. 2010) on its own, within 0.3–1.6 km. Earth positions agree with an independent method (Meeus) to within 0.03°. 61 automated tests pass.

Tools

Python (NumPy, SciPy, Skyfield, rasterio, FastAPI), JavaScript (Plotly.js, Three.js), GitHub Pages.

Benefits and goals

Faster, clearer and explainable landing decisions, free and accessible on any phone or computer.

Limits and next steps

The map covers 120 × 120 km at 160 m resolution, and communication means line of sight only. Next: wider and finer terrain, a full link-budget and DSN model, and Artemis III / CLPS site lists.
